item.title: Pakistan secure fifth Asian Games medal with PUBG Mobile bronze
item.description:
Pakistan won their fifth medal of the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Tuesday when their PUBG Mobile team secured bronze in the esports competition at the Aichi Sky Expo in Tokoname.

Pakistan finished third in the 12-match competition with 100 points, behind gold medallists Thailand, who accumulated 128 points, and China, who took silver with 114.

The bronze came after Pakistan finished third in the final match of the competition, scoring 12 points — four placement points and eight elimination points. Japan won the match with 18 points, while Thailand finished second with 14.

Pakistan’s medal tally at the Games now comprises five bronzes — the women’s cricket team, modern MMA fighter Asim Khan, squash players Noor Zaman and Ashab Irfan, and the PUBG Mobile team.

The women’s cricket team secured its medal on Sept 22 by defeating Bangladesh by 31 runs, while Noor and Ashab both guaranteed bronze medals by reaching the men’s singles squash semi-finals before losing their respective last-four matches.

Pakistan’s PUBG Mobile team, comprising Mohammad Huzaifa, Shayan Asad, Falak Sher, Hasnain Rehman and Syed Sameer, finished strongly after entering the second day of competition in medal contention.

They collected 61 points across the final six matches to finish on 100, having accumulated 39 on the opening day.

Pakistan’s best returns on the second day included 16 points in the seventh match, 10 each in the eighth and ninth, 12 in the 11th and 12 in the concluding match.

Thailand’s consistency throughout the competition saw them finish 28 points clear of Pakistan, while China held off the Pakistani challenge for silver by 14 points.

Vietnam and Indonesia finished level on 95 points, followed by South Korea on 71, Chinese Taipei on 62 and Jordan on 61.

The medal adds another sport to Pakistan’s growing haul at the Games and marks a podium finish for the country in an esports discipline.

PUBG Mobile was contested as one of the esports medal events at the Games, with 12 teams competing in the final over two days. The competition was decided on aggregate points from the 12 matches.

Pakistan volleyball push Japan to brink

Pakistan’s volleyball team ended their Pool A campaign with a 3-0 defeat to hosts Japan at the Okazaki Chuo Sogo Park Gymnasium on Tuesday, but not before pushing the tournament favourites to the brink in a fiercely contested opening set.

Japan won 29-27, 25-20, 25-22 in a match that lasted one hour and 23 minutes.

The first set was the highlight of the contest. Pakistan matched Japan point for point, forcing the set beyond 25 and saving multiple set points before the hosts finally edged it 29-27 after 29 minutes of play. It was the closest any side has come to taking a set off Japan in the pool stage.

The hosts asserted control in the second set, taking it 25-20 in 26 minutes, before closing out the match 25-22 in the third.

Pakistan’s outside hitter Ali Usman led the scoring with 13 points, while Musawer Khan added 11 and opposite Murad Khan contributed 10.

Japan finished with 79 total points to Pakistan’s 69, though the statistics showed how evenly matched the sides were. Japan edged the spikes 89-86, but Pakistan led the reception battle 62-60. Both teams registered three service points, and Japan committed more errors, 23 to Pakistan’s 19.

Pakistan won their opening game against Kazakhstan 3-1 before defeating Uzbekistan 3-0 on Monday. Their final standing in Pool A will be confirmed once the remaining fixtures are completed.

Two defeats in a day

Pakistan’s women’s squash team played two matches on Tuesday, losing to South Korea in their Pool B fixture before also going down to Macao, China in the stage 1 round-robin at the Nagoya Kinjo Futo Arena.

Against South Korea, the trio of Mahnoor Ali, Sana Bahadur and Mehwish Ali all lost in straight games.

Mahnoor, 13, faced the 30-year-old Hwayeong Eum in the first tie, but experience prevailed over flair as the South Korean won 11-2, 11-4, 11-7 in 18 minutes.

The responsibility of pulling Pakistan back into the match then fell to Sana, but the 20-year-old could not deliver, losing to Mingyeong Heo 11-5, 11-5, 11-8 in 19 minutes.

With the tie already decided, Mehwish still tried to register a consolation win, only to be denied by Dami Kim 11-3, 11-8, 11-5.

Later in the round-robin stage against Macao, Mahnoor again lost her opening match, going down to Wain Leng Yeung 11-9, 11-3, 12-10.

Sana started strongly, winning the first game 11-4 against Weng Chi Yeung, but the 25-year-old Macao player took the next three 11-6, 11-7, 11-6 to seal the match.

Sehrish replaced her sister Mehwish for the third match but could not change Pakistan’s fortunes, losing a tight contest to Chi Cheng Cao 4-11, 13-11, 15-13, 11-7.

Pakistan had opened with a 3-0 loss to Hong Kong on Monday before beating Mongolia by the same margin later that day.

Rain delay costs Shoaib

At the Higashiyama Park Tennis Centre, Mohammad Shoaib’s campaign in the men’s singles ended as he lost 6-4, 6-4 to Indonesia’s Rifqi Fitriadi in the round-of-32.

The match had been suspended on Monday with Shoaib leading the first set 4-3, and the overnight break proved costly as Fitriadi returned on Tuesday to complete the win in one hour and eight minutes of play.

Fitriadi edged the statistical battle, winning 74 total points to Shoaib’s 65. The Indonesian also held a slight advantage in aces, striking four to Shoaib’s three, while both players committed two double faults.

Shoaib then returned to partner Aqeel Khan in the men’s doubles against Chinese Taipei’s Yu-hsiou Hsu and Chenjui Ho, but the pair lost 6-3, 6-2.

item.title: 'Non-lethal': How India and Israel's brutal use of pellet guns spread worldwide
item.description:
'Non-lethal': How India and Israel's brutal use of pellet guns spread worldwide

Submitted by Anuradha Bhasin on Wed, 09/23/2026 - 11:36
The real danger isn't in how these lethal technologies, including pellet guns, are exported and shared; the greater peril is in the precedent their use against civilian protesters sets
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) supporters wave national flags a day after the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in Mumbai, India, 26 July 2026 (Punit Paranjape/AFP)
On

In July 2026, Amnesty International published a report Made in India: the supply of weapons and munitions to Israel. It found India shipped hundreds of thousands of weapon parts and munitions components to Israel throughout its Gaza offensive, and it warned the exports carry a "substantial risk" of contributing to what it calls Israel's "ongoing genocide".

The real danger isn't only in how these lethal technologies are exported and shared. The greater peril is in the wrong precedent their use against civilians sets.

A telling example is the use of pellet guns by police in Delhi to control a student’s march to the Indian parliament in protest against an examination leak scam, which injured at least 10 civilians, including a young man who may lose his vision forever. 

The journey of the use of pellet guns for crowd control from Kashmir to New Delhi reminds us that any battleground is always a testing ground. What gets legitimised in one place does not stay there. 

India introduced pellet guns in 2010 in Kashmir and framed it as a "non-lethal" or "less-lethal" weapon for crowd control. Between 2010 and 2019, 24 people were killed. Most casualties happened after their widespread use to control violent protests following the death of militant commander Burhan Wani, who was killed in an encounter in 2016. Between July 2016 and February 2019, metal pellets killed 18 people, blinded 139, and resulted in 2,942 injuries, of which 1,459 were serious eye injuries. 

A pellet gun is a .12-bore pump-action shotgun, normally used in bird hunting, that fires a cartridge loaded with several hundred metal pellets that disperse over a wide area rather than travelling as a single projectile.

Each cartridge holds up to several hundred small pellets. On firing, the pellets scatter outward in a wide spray at about 100-150 metres per second. Because of this spread, one shot can strike multiple people in a crowd at once.

In short, it doesn’t choose its target. It can hit anyone within that range. The enormous scale of injuries, even deaths, caused by pellets in Kashmir and the people they hit - a girl sitting by her window, a baby in her mother’s arms - made no distinction between allegedly violent protesters and those who just happened to be in the wrong place at the wrong moment.

Opening old wounds

The brutality of the pellet guns cannot be fully comprehended without understanding how the lives of the majority of the victims are scarred forever. 

Despite the "less-lethal" tag, the pellets are sharp enough to pierce the skin and stay embedded in the body, causing permanent pain in some cases. On occasion, they have caused permanent blindness. The psychological wounds they inflict are irreparable. There have also been cases of injuries resulting in deaths. 

Yet, the use of pellet guns in Kashmir was justified under a manufactured broad consensus built entirely through a security prism. 

The state embraced the weapon, framing it as "non-lethal", despite documentary evidence of hundreds blinded, scores killed, and many others permanently disabled. It invited no uproar or outrage. This nationwide tendency to see Kashmir as a state of exception has also encouraged a shameful mocking of its victims - the latest example being the forthcoming Bollywood film Chauhaan. 

It was used with the bland justification: terrorism, national security. This, even as there is no documentary evidence of the weapon ever being used against insurgents - only on civilian protesters. A security doctrine, borrowed from international playbooks, and built for a region on the pretext of insurgency, is now being exported. 

History of violence

Before its use in Delhi, pellet guns were used during the farmers’ protest and in Manipur. Their use in Delhi against protesting students evoked nationwide outrage, with the framing "they were students, not terrorists’". That framing never extends to the community the national imagination has already conflated with terrorists - Kashmir, Manipur and Punjab (whose farmers led the protests). The presumption of innocence isn't universal. It is assigned by identity.

Lethal weapon: How Bollywood's 'Chauhaan' trivialises the suffering of Kashmiris maimed by Indian forces
Read More »

Far more problematic is the state response that is still relying on old tactics of skirting questions about pellet injuries. It has moved from denial to deflection but no accountability.

As opposition leaders led by Congress, a party that ironically introduced pellet guns in 2010, are uniting and demanding answers to who ordered the pellet guns and why, India’s home minister Amit Shah has refused to attend parliament. 

Zero accountability automatically translates to a continuum of use of pellet guns or other weapons framed as "non-lethal’". In Kashmir, there is a documented record of young men killed when tear gas shells were directly aimed at their upper bodies in 2010. 

Even the Supreme Court has refused a total ban on the use of pellet guns and has deflected the question to examining the gaps between standard operating procedures and realities on the ground. The debate on whether lethal weapons can be used for crowd control is incomplete if restricted to these issues.

The debate also needs to take into account the impact of weapons that are projected as "non-lethal" or "less-lethal" but kill people nonetheless. It needs to weigh up the fact that a bad precedent travels from one geography to another and beyond borders.

Lethal export

Pellet guns have already travelled the globe. The United Kingdom is the first known country to have deployed shotguns with rubber and plastic pellets during the Troubles, the 30-year violent conflict in Northern Ireland, and inspired the United States police to adopt similar versions of the weapon for crowd control.

Pellet guns are just another demonstration of how quickly any state learns that civilians can be treated as acceptable targets once the first wrongful justification goes unchallenged

Pellet guns, along with other so-called "non-lethal" weapons, have been used with impunity in Palestine. Whether India borrowed this method of repression from Israel or not, the list of countries now using it to target their own citizens is growing.

In Chile in 2019, 230 people lost their vision. Bangladesh used it in 2024, killing 22 student protesters and blinding 400. They were used in the recent Iran protests, with at least 74 documented cases of pellet injuries in vital parts of the body. A man’s lung was damaged by 174 pellets tightly packed inside his right chest cavity.  

The pellet guns are just another demonstration of how quickly any state learns that civilians can be treated as acceptable targets once the first wrongful justification goes unchallenged.

Nuclear strikes may be a rare exception, but there are enough examples, like the use of white phosphorous and drone air strikes that reveal a brutal truth: what is used in one place doesn’t stay there; it travels wherever the next authority wants the same cover of impunity.

item.title: Malaysia starts sending Myanmar migrants home
item.description:
Malaysia began sending back around 1,500 Myanmar nationals Tuesday, AFP journalists saw, launching a scheme rights groups say may endanger migrants by returning them to the war-torn country.

The batch is the first of 5,000 Myanmar citizens Kuala Lumpur says agreed to “voluntary” repatriation from detention centres amidst a huge uptick in anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia.

But advocacy organisations say dire conditions in detention centres may have forced their decisions, and they could face dangerous homecomings in Myanmar where war has raged since 2021.

Neither Malaysia nor Myanmar have officially clarified the number of Rohingya in the first group, and there is concern they may be returned to a country where they face persecution rights groups say amounts to genocide.

Dozens of buses arrived under police escort on Tuesday at the Majlis Perbandaran Manjung stadium near the Lumut naval base in northwestern Malaysia, AFP correspondents saw, where the migrants were to be processed.

They will then be transported to the nearby naval base and taken to Myanmar by ship.

A Myanmar security source, requesting anonymity because they were not authorised to talk to media, said the boats are due to dock at Thanlyin Navy Base just south of Yangon around the end of this week.

Marine traffic websites showed Myanmar’s auxiliary support and hospital ship Than Lwin at anchor just outside the naval base.

Rohingya, a persecuted Muslim minority, make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the United Nations.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced in July that Myanmar had agreed to take back 5,000 members of the Rohingya.

‘Safe’ return promised

The plan was announced after authorities detained more than 100 Rohingya who had gathered outside the UN refugee agency’s office in Kuala Lumpur.

They were seeking help after being threatened with eviction from an informal settlement in northern Penang state.

They were later released after officials confirmed they held valid UN documentation.

Myanmar earlier this month pledged “safe and dignified” returns for its citizens displaced abroad, after criticism from the United Nations and rights groups.

Last week, more than 160 civil society groups in a joint statement called upon the Malaysian government to “immediately halt the deportations,” pending talks with civil organisations about the situation on the ground in Myanmar.

Anwar said he would invite Myanmar’s coup leader-turned-civilian president Min Aung Hlaing for an official visit to help expedite the repatriation process.

But the civil groups urged that “Malaysia’s engagement with the junta must not come at the expense of its own reputation and integrity.”

Malaysia’s home affairs ministry last month said 5,000 individuals will undergo voluntary repatriation as agreed by the Myanmar government.

There were 10,388 Myanmar nationals held at immigration detention depots by mid-August, the ministry said, with not all considered refugees.

Malaysia, which shelters one of Southeast Asia’s biggest refugee populations, is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention and does not formally recognise refugee status.

AFP fact-checkers have found that Rohingya refugees in Malaysia have been targeted by online disinformation campaigns that rights advocates say are fuelling xenophobia and intimidation.

Many of the Rohingya, a mostly Muslim group, escaped Myanmar during a brutal military crackdown in 2017.

Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled Myanmar after the offensive, which is the basis of a genocide case at the International Court of Justice.

More than 1.2 million live just over the border in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement, but talk of repatriations from there has yielded little progress.

item.title: Bangladesh, Sri Lanka through to Asiad semis after rain washes out quarter-finals
item.description:
Sri Lanka and Bangladesh reached the semi-finals of the men’s cricket competition of the Asian Games on Tuesday without a ball being bowled following more wet weather in Nagoya.

The Sri Lankans will meet India in the last four and Bangladesh play Pakistan, with both matches scheduled for Thursday.

Organisers are now racing to get the converted baseball field at Korogi Athletic Park ready in time.

Sri Lanka progressed when their quarter-final with Nepal was washed out – higher-ranked teams go through in the event of a wash out or no-result.

Bangladesh were awarded victory over lower-ranked Malaysia for the same reason.

Pakistan and reigning champions India sealed their semi-final spots after rain also washed out both matches on Monday, against Hong Kong and Afghanistan respectively.

“Cricket, like baseball, you can’t play it in the rain,” said Jarrad Shearer, who is in charge of the cricket tournament.

There has been heavy rain in Games host Nagoya and Aichi prefecture in recent days, but better weather is forecast from Wednesday.

“Come tomorrow morning, it will be all hands on deck to dry up the areas that aren’t under the covers,” said Shearer.

“We’ve got some soppers, we’ve got some squeegees, some big old brooms, we’ve got sponges.

“Plus it’s supposed to be sunny and 32 degrees Celsius, so with any luck we’ll soak up as much water as we can in the morning and the sun will do its work in the afternoon.”

item.title: Greek EU presidency eyes migrant return hub in Africa: Minister
item.description:
Greece said Monday it aimed to set up a hub in Africa for sending back migrants once it takes up the EU presidency in 2027.

"We believe that the framework is opening up under the Greek presidency for the return centre to operate," Greece's migration minister Thanos Plevris told ANT1 TV.

He added that the hub would run "in an African country that we have already agreed on; we simply cannot name it yet."

Greece will hold the rotating presidency of the European Union in the second half of 2027.

Uganda and Rwanda have been cited as possible sites, with EU states Denmark, Austria, Germany and the Netherlands working with Greece on the initiative.

Plevris said a meeting will soon be organised with the other four EU states and the director of the International Organisation for Migration to discuss the plan.

The European Parliament in June approved a regulation on the return of migrants whose asylum claims have been rejected, including the possibility for member states to conclude agreements to establish detention centres outside the union's borders.

This regulation, intended to speed up expulsions, has raised concerns among human rights advocates.

The Council of Europe, the continent's human rights watchdog, has sent letters to the commissioners responsible for migration policy in these five countries, submitting recommendations to them to address potential human rights violations.

Plevris also said that Greece wants to present at the next European Council on Home Affairs on 1 October "a mechanism of exceptional measures" in the event of an influx crisis such as the recent events in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, where 72,000 migrants crossed the border from Morocco.

"In times of crisis, measures outside the box must be taken," he said.

"In these cases where we have instrumentalisation (of migration), and we have experienced it with mass flows that we have prevented, then not only should asylum not even be considered, there should be an immediate issuance of a return decision and immediate return," Plevris said.

Greece has twice suspended the registration of asylum applications: in March 2020 during a crisis at the Greek-Turkish border, and in July 2025 during a large influx to Crete of migrants coming from Libya.

item.title: Banglalink brings mobile services to ChatGPT
item.description:
Banglalink has brought its core mobile services into ChatGPT in the first such integration by a telecom operator in Bangladesh, allowing customers to access everyday mobile services through a simple conversation, reports a press release.

With Banglalink GPT, subscribers can manage everyday telco needs directly through ChatGPT, from checking their balance and usage and finding suitable packs to checking roaming status and accessing other key mobile services, without having to switch between different apps or websites.

Developed by Banglalink Digital, the service is now live nationwide for Banglalink subscribers. They can find Banglalink GPT in ChatGPT’s GPT section and use it by simply asking questions in everyday language.

Banglalink GPT also recommends suitable packs to users based on their needs and usage. For instance, a customer planning to watch a movie can ask which pack would be suitable, while another can ask to check their current balance, minutes or internet data.

Customers can also check their roaming status through the assistant. For services that require a transaction, customers can complete the process through Banglalink’s payment portal.

Taimur Rahman, chief corporate & regulatory affairs Officer of Banglalink, said, “Customer expectations are evolving rapidly as AI becomes increasingly integrated into everyday life. At Banglalink, we believe that accessing and managing mobile services should evolve accordingly. By becoming the first telecom operator in Bangladesh to bring our services into ChatGPT, we are making it easier for customers to discover, manage, and purchase the services they need through a familiar conversational interface. This initiative reflects our commitment to using technology to make digital experiences more intuitive, accessible, and customer-centric”

The new service is part of Banglalink’s broader effort as a digital operator to make everyday services simpler and more accessible through technology.

item.title: Salauddin: No journalist to be victimized under Cyber Security law
item.description:
The government is exercising utmost caution so that the proposed Cyber Security (Amendment) Act does not become an oppressive law and that no journalist or media outlet is victimized under it, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said on Monday.
The proposed law would be finalized only after extensive consultations with stakeholders and consideration of their recommendations, he said at a press briefing at the Secretariat following a consultation meeting with representatives of print and electronic media at the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.
“Our primary objective is to ensure that no journalist falls victim to the misuse of this law,” he said.
The home minister said the draft amendment bill was earlier laid before the Cabinet, which directed the authorities to hold extensive discussions with IT experts and other stakeholders involved in cyberspace.
Then the government published the draft on its website to seek opinions from people from all walks of life, he said, adding that feedback has already been received from various institutions, human rights organisations, students and cyberspace users.
Monday’s meeting was the government’s second consultation with editors, senior journalists, newspaper organisations and representatives of professional journalists’ associations.
At the first meeting on September 10, editors were requested to submit their views in writing or through the website.
The minister said many participants presented their views at Monday’s meeting and pledged to submit written recommendations.
He said a proposal came to hold detailed discussions between media and cyber experts to ensure that the media is not harmed or victimised and that necessary safeguards are incorporated into the law.
“The government has gladly accepted the proposal,” Salahuddin said, adding that the government has no intention of enacting the law to target the media.
Regarding safeguards for journalists in print, electronic and online media, the minister said a proposal was made to make prior court approval mandatory before taking action against or arresting a journalist.
He said the government considered the proposal appropriate and logical.
Stakeholders will be given another 15 days to submit formal recommendations, which will then be considered for inclusion in the draft, he said.
A provision setting a specific timeframe for the disposal of cases or appeals will also be considered to prevent people from remaining in legal uncertainty for an indefinite period, the minister added.
Salahuddin said a special coordination mechanism would be formed to help finalise the draft.
The Principal Information Officer will serve as the focal point, while the Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology and the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting will jointly coordinate the process.
Representatives of the Editors’ Council, Electronic Media Association and a panel of cyber experts formed by the IT ministry will participate in the process and are expected to submit recommendations within 7 to 15 days, said the minister.
The revised draft will then be published on the government website again for further public feedback before being placed before the Cabinet, the minister added.
If the recommendations are accepted, they will be incorporated into the draft before an inter-ministerial review and submission to the Cabinet.
After Cabinet approval, the bill will be placed before Parliament where it will undergo further deliberation involving members of both the ruling and opposition parties as well as views emerging from seminars and symposiums outside Parliament.
Salahuddin said the main objective of the proposed law is to establish a balanced legal framework to protect the country, society and young people from cybercrimes and other criminal activities.
The act is also intended to comply with international standards while protecting social and religious harmony, family values and indigenous culture, he said.

item.title: 4,585 SSC, equivalent exam candidates pass after re-scrutiny
item.description:
A total of 4,585 candidates who initially failed the SSC and equivalent examinations in 2026 have passed after their answer scripts were re-scrutinised and re-evaluated.
In addition, 3,079 candidates received new GPAs.
The Ministry of Education released the statistics on the results of the re-scrutiny and re-evaluation on Monday.
According to ministry data, a total of 1,829,485 candidates appeared for the SSC and equivalent examinations. Of them, 402,052 candidates applied for re-scrutiny and re-evaluation of their answer scripts.
Among the answer scripts submitted for review, 1,056,455 were theoretical scripts and 231,471 were practical scripts. A total of 1,287,926 scripts were re-scrutinised.
The results showed grade changes for 27,836 candidates, while the marks of 56,259 candidates were changed.

item.title: Bangladesh lose to Singapore 1-0 in Asean Cup
item.description:
Bangladesh suffered a 1-0 defeat to Singapore in their second Group A match of the FIFA Asean Cup 2026 at the Gelora Bung Karno Stadium in Jakarta, Indonesia, on Monday.
Harhys Stewart scored the only goal in the first half, which proved decisive as Singapore secured their third straight victory over Bangladesh.
Following a cross from Nur Adam Abdullah, Harhys headed home in the 35th minute after Bangladesh goalkeeper Mehedi Hasan Srabon had made a couple of important saves.
Srabon first denied Ilhan Fandi with a diving save in the 17th minute before rescuing Bangladesh from a goalmouth scramble in the 33rd minute.
The men in red and green piled on the pressure in search of an equaliser throughout the second half but could not find the net, with headers from Shamit Shome and Saad Uddin missing the target.
Shamit's flying header from a Saad cross went over the bar, while Saad headed wide from substitute Fahamedul Islam's cross. Hamza Choudhury was pushed further forward in the closing stages, but Bangladesh could not find a way through.
Bangladesh coach Thomas Dooley made three changes to the starting XI that lost 3-0 to Malaysia in their tournament opener on Friday.
Centre-back Zidane Yousuf and midfielder Jamal Bhuiyan came into the lineup in place of Shakil Ahad Topu and Sohel Rana, while Sheikh Morsalin replaced Farhaan Ali Wahid, who made his international debut against Malaysia, in the forward line.
In the second half, Minhaz Shadin replaced Morsalin to make his international debut.

item.title: BCB unveils annual domestic competition spanning three formats
item.description:
The Bangladesh Cricket Board unveiled a new three-format domestic tournament that will bring together T20, 50-over and four-day cricket under a single competition in an effort to increase interest in the country’s domestic game.
The tournament, called the Domestic Three Trophy, or D3 Trophy, will feature six teams owned by six corporate groups under three-year agreements with the BCB.
The six teams are backed by H. Bluestar, Walton Group, Citizens Bank, ACME Group, Seven Rings Cement and Fortune Group. The team owners include three BCB directors: Fahim Sinha of ACME Group, Mizanur Rahman of Fortune Group and Shahniyan Tanim of H. Bluestar.
The D3 Trophy will replace three of the BCB’s existing domestic competitions with a single structure. The four-day National Cricket League will remain separate, while the Bangladesh Cricket League’s four-day and one-day competitions and the NCL’s T20 competition will be incorporated into the new tournament.
The T20 competition will open the tournament on Dec. 15 at the renovated Jibanananda Das Cricket Stadium in Barishal. The BCB plans to gradually take the competition to all divisions. Khulna is being considered as the second venue, with Dhaka as an alternative.
The four-day matches will begin in January, followed by the 50-over competition in May. Across the three formats, the tournament will feature seven four-day matches, 16 one-day matches and 19 T20 matches.
Each team will be allowed to sign up to 23 players for all three formats. Coaching staff, analysts, physiotherapists and trainers will also be selected through a draft.
The six teams announced their icon players at Sunday’s launch. Walton selected Mehedi Hasan Miraz, Fortune chose Towhid Hridoy, ACME took Mosaddek Hossain, Seven Rings Cement picked Mushfiqur Rahim, H. Bluestar selected Nurul Hasan and Citizens Bank named Mohammad Naim.
BCB President Tamim Iqbal said the board had been concerned by criticism that domestic cricket had lost its appeal.
“We often hear that domestic cricket has lost its color, that there is no interest and that some call it picnic cricket,” he said. “When we came to the board, we were concerned about this and thought about how we could bring that color back.”
Youth and Sports State Minister Aminul Haque said keeping domestic cricket active for six or seven months a year could help narrow the gap between players competing at domestic level and those in the national team.

item.title: Netherlands regrets Israel retaliation in settlements row
item.description:
The Netherlands said Monday it regretted Israel’s decision to revoke accreditation of Dutch diplomats based in the West Bank, the latest retaliation by Israel to mounting Western pressure over settlements.
Israel, which has occupied the West Bank since 1967 and exerts power over diplomats’ entry into the Palestinian territory, on Monday ordered Dutch officials to surrender their diplomatic privileges.
“I deeply regret this unnecessary decision,” Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen said.
Israel retaliated after Dutch authorities began implementing a ban on imports of any products from Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
The decision, Berendsen said, was “not directed against Israel.”
The minister said the suspension of the imports came from “the obligation, under international law, not to contribute to an unlawful situation: the illegal settlements.”
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar, announcing the move on Sunday, vowed: “Any country that acts in a hostile and one-sided manner against Israel will lose its influence and relevance in the region.”
“If the Netherlands wishes to continue representing its interests vis-a-vis the Palestinians, it may do so from the territory of the Palestinian Authority and not from the territory of the State of Israel,” he said.
Israel controls entry points into the West Bank and the Oslo peace accords in the 1990s gave Israel control over diplomatic accreditation in the Palestinian territories.
The Palestinian Authority condemned the move, saying Israel was trying to “reduce the international and diplomatic presence in Palestine so that it can carry out its crimes without witnesses.”
“The State of Palestine affirms that Dutch diplomats are welcome on the territory of the occupied State of Palestine, and that Israel has no sovereignty over any part of the land of the State of Palestine,” the foreign ministry said.
The Dutch government imposed the sanctions in July out of alarm at the rising number of attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians and talk by Israeli politicians of formally annexing the territory.
Britain, France and Canada also announced in early September that they would impose sanctions on trade from Israeli settlements. Israel responded by ordering the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem.
Ahead of Israeli elections on October 27, opposition figure Yair Lapid, a centrist former prime minister, said that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu bore responsibility for the “anti-Israel wave.”
“The fact that Israelis landing in the Netherlands are having their bags rummaged through and products from the settlements confiscated is a diplomatic failure unlike anything we have seen before,” Lapid said, promising improved diplomacy but not mentioning a change in policy on settlements.
The United Nations says extremist settlers have been responsible for an average of six attacks per day on Palestinians and Palestinian property in the West Bank in 2026.
Palestinians have also attacked Israelis, with a Palestinian shooting dead a settler last week and a car-ramming attack seriously injuring the soldier son of the Israeli ambassador to Washington.

item.title: Death toll in South Africa bar shooting rises to 18
item.description:
The death toll in a mass shooting in a South African tavern has risen to 18 after one person died in hospital, police said Monday, adding that at least two of the dead were Lesotho nationals.
The shooting west of Johannesburg late Saturday was part of a bloody weekend in the crime-weary country, with 10 people killed in another mass shooting in Cape Town on Sunday.
Eight gunmen armed with assault rifles stormed the bar in the semi-rural township of Wedela, around 80 kilometers (50 miles) from central Johannesburg, killing 13 men and four women, police said.
“One more victim has died in hospital, bringing the total number of deceased to 18,” they said Monday. Eighteen people were wounded.
“Only four of the deceased have been identified, two South Africans and two Lesotho nationals.”
The motive for the attack was not clear, but police said it may have been retaliation for an incident in the same tavern in August when one person was killed and another wounded.
The area was gripped by rivalry between gangs involved in illicit mining for gold, the tavern owner told local journalists at the scene, where bloodied clothes lay on the ground.
“Even if they finish investigating, I am scared to continue selling again. I am too scared,” she said, hiding her identity.
Thousands of unregistered miners operate in abandoned mining shafts in South Africa, in a sector linked to organized crime, assassinations and other illegal activities.
Many come from across southern Africa, including the kingdom of Lesotho which is embedded within South Africa.
In a separate shooting at the weekend, gunmen killed 10 people and wounded 11 more at an eating and drinking venue in a township outside Cape Town early on Sunday.
In video clips shared on social media, revelers can be seen dancing and drinking before a burst of gunfire rings out, sending people scrambling for cover.
Police said it was not clear what prompted the attack in Lwandle, but one official said it may have been business rivalry.
There had been no arrests in either of the mass killings.
South Africa is awash with legal and illegal firearms and shootings are common. The country of around 62 million people has one of the world’s highest murder rates, with about 60 people killed each day.
There have been at least 41 mass killings this year at the cost of 196 lives, said Julian Rademeyer, an adviser for the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC).
“Very often these are killings that are linked to organized crime” including illegal mining, gang violence and extortion, he told the Newzroom Afrika broadcaster.
In March, President Cyril Ramaphosa deployed the army to violence hotspots around Johannesburg and Cape Town after describing organized crime the “most immediate threat” to South Africa’s democracy and economic development.
The weekend bloodshed further rattled South Africans already alarmed by the discovery of the bodies of 11 women, one of them on Sunday, in 10 weeks in Johannesburg’s Ekurhuleni area.
Most of the victims were in their 20s and 30s, with some found stripped of their clothes and showing signs of sexual assault, police said.
In the same area, a 23-year-old woman was shot and killed early Monday during an alleged robbery while she was on the way to work, police said.
“Preliminary investigations have not established any link between this incident and the recent cases involving the bodies of women found in Ekurhuleni,” they said in a statement.

item.title: Two dead, 14 missing after avalanche on Nepal’s Himlung peak
item.description:
At least two people have been killed and 14 remain missing after an avalanche at Nepal’s Himlung peak, an official said on Monday, as rescuers resumed their search.
The avalanche swept through the base camp of the 7,126-metre (23,345-foot) peak near the Chinese border early on Sunday, burying tents under deep snow.
“Two bodies were found as rescuers worked until 6pm last night,” Tul Singh Gurung, president of the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association, told AFP.
“The search continues for 14 expedition workers who are still missing.”
A team of eight mountain guides is involved in the search operation, he added.
Mountaineer Mingma G Sherpa, who is leading the rescue team, said challenging weather conditions were hampering their efforts.
“We could have saved lives but due to bad weather, we reached the accident site only in the evening (on Sunday),” he wrote on Facebook.
Sherpa said the deceased were both guides, while the 14 missing were kitchen staff working at the expedition camp.
Organizers initially reported that at least 10 people were missing.
It was the latest natural disaster to hit Nepal in recent weeks.
The Himalayan nation is rebuilding from a devastating glacial flood on August 26 that killed more than 1,400 people and left over 6,000 missing.
And heavy rain since Thursday has triggered other floods and landslides, killing at least 21 people, according to the national disaster agency.
Home to eight of the world’s 14 highest peaks, Nepal relies heavily on mountaineering and trekking tourism.

item.description:
“Twenty years ago, the state of North Dakota poured in multiple millions of dollars to figure out what it looks like to do beyond visual line-of-sight operations for Class One, Two, and Three Drones. That was just the very nascent stage. Just a decade ago, ten years ago, they figured out that they can do this. They could do this at Grand Forks Air Force Base. Right across from our [air base] runway, on the active duty side, is a place called Grand Sky. It is an innovation research park for all counter-drone operations. It is one of the largest in the United States. They rent the space on our base. It's legitimately federal property that they lease for the research park.”

That was Air Force Col. Alfred J. Rosales, Commander, 319th Reconnaissance Wing, based at Grand Forks Air Force Base, speaking on September 14, at the 2026 Air, Space & Cyber Conference, as moderator of a panel on Counter-Drone Defense.

I had never heard about what the Grand Forks locals call GrandSKY as a home for Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS), where for a decade major defense contractors such as Northrop Grumman and General Atomics have been flight testing and carrying out drone research and development.

Back in May, the Defense Department’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401, central authority for the counter-small unmanned aircraft systems program, selected five installations to participate in the directed-energy counter-unmanned aircraft systems pilot program, of which Grand Forks was one.

More recently, as Rosales put it, at the Grand Forks Base, they have been “strapping on vendor equipment” to “build tactics and techniques.” That process will help determine, he said, “How do we want directed-energy weapons to be used inside the United States in FAA [Federal Aviation Agency] controlled airspace, not in the restricted ranges of our Air Force.”

Rosales introduced his September 14, panel whom he said were industry leaders who were “translating technology into trust to allow us to win in the future.”

They were:

Dr. Ben Van Roo, Chief Executive Officer, Legion Intelligence, who, using Artificial Intelligence (AI) was working to get the equipment needed at the tactical level to be able to provide decision-making space without being connected to the Cloud the entire time.

Early on Van Roo said, “We're really still in the infancy right now of how we think about where we're going to use [computer] agents [AI]. What are we going to allow them to decide on? How do they work their way into our TTPs [Tactics, Techniques and Procedures] into our doctrine? And then, the other side, and the big question that we also think about is are they even going to be available?”

Van Roo continued, “The way that we want to use Artificial Intelligence is going to be one, it's still got to be sorted out. What are we going to allow these things [AI] decide to do? Where are they going to work? Into everything from the kill chain to just basic intelligence gathering? And then how are we going to make them more resilient? These are the next layers of challenges that are ahead of us.”

Adam Mohamed, Chief Technology Officer, Asylon Robotics, a Boston Dynamics Partner, who works on autonomous robotics, figuring out how we can layer base defense architecture with our air domain experts.

“Situational awareness is king,” Mohamed said, “because everything else flows from that. And having static situation awareness, mobile situational awareness, being able to understand your battle space is going to take precedence over everything else. The sensor fusion will happen. We'll have the AI. We'll have the ability to operate without a Cloud. But we need to be able to operate when we start losing our sensors, we start losing our radars, we start losing our shooters, and how do we adapt and how does the system adapt for you, because there won't be time for you to make the change to switch over.”

Colton Wood, Chief Technology Officer, Digital Force Technologies, who works on multi-sensor integration. How do we use AI to get the common operating pictures we so desperately desire -- the integration piece that's going to help defeat drones.

Wood said, “Talking about human in the loop is okay. I got a target, I need to go through the process of actually engaging and affecting that target. As we see the threat evolving, that is going to be an incredibly difficult thing to do if I have, you know, multiple threats, multiple targets, multiple different engagement systems…I've set all the rules of engagement. I've set the governance on the systems and then I have a strong decision supported by tools in front of me. But once I've made that decision, I need to be able to engage the systems and machines need to be able to engage the threats, almost autonomously.”

Therefore, Wood explained, “And so I think a lot of simulations, understanding how these systems operate, where the left and right limits are and then allowing these systems to be as effective as they can be without us having to shepherd the process is a very thing that we have to think about [in the] very near future here.”

And finally, Michael Hiatt, Chief Technology Officer, Epirus, who works with Directed-Energy weapons, lasers, the essence of kill-chain dynamics. He comes with skill sets on how to integrate and work in that space.

Hiatt said, “Your risk is very different if you have to literally put metal [kinetic weapons] in the air, you know, with kinetics or, you know, proximate-burst rounds or whatever the kinetic options are. If you can have an option that has lower collateral effects and no collateral damage, you know, which is what the Directed-Energy [DE, laser] weapons offer, you start to be able to change your risk calculation.”


Hiatt continued, “But when for the folks that are on the ground, you know, the battle captain trying to trying to make that assessment, it's not a cost asymmetry problem. It's a magazine depth issue because, you know, what's the reload time on my kinetic? What's the, you know, what's the fly-out time? How many do I, you know, what's my shot doctrine? Do I do a shoot, look, shoot? Do I do a shoot, shoot, look? You know, those are the things that affect magazine consumption.”

Hiatt added, “The reality is you know DE weapons aren't out-ranging kinetic [weapons]. And so when you start to say, ‘All right, I'm going to hold fire on my kinetics. I'm going to let that threat come in closer than I would like because I trust that my DE weapons are going to take it out.’ That's the level of trust that we got to get to.”

At the end of the 41-minute session, Col. Rosales tried to sum it up saying, “This space in counter drones is not a spectator sport. It's for all of us to think through it, industry, academia, the United States Air Force. What I hear is that we are beyond asking what these things are, AI agents, as they incorporate into this picture. We're at the point where we're figuring out what it could look like in terms of policy [so] that we can then get to the next step -- in training and exercising with a rigor to ensure that we have the trust to have our airmen engage when those courses of action are recommended.”

My guess is we are nowhere close to deciding policies where AI fits into the counter-drone fight, nor in warfare itself.

item.title: Bangladesh women lose ground after quota reform
item.description:
Bangladesh’s 2024 student-led uprising was fuelled by a demand that coveted government jobs be awarded on merit, not through quotas.

The movement succeeded, the government was overthrown, and the quota system was largely scrapped — but the reform has had unintended consequences.

Women are securing a shrinking share of public sector jobs in the Muslim-majority nation of 170 million people.

Tothapi Azad, a 25-year-old Dhaka University graduate, supported calls to end quotas — but says she should have supported retaining them for women.

“For me, who had my family’s support, a quota might not have been essential — but for an average woman, it was essential,” she told AFP.

“A job is a tool for women’s empowerment. For rural women, it is more than that — a survival tactic, a shield to resist domestic violence.”

Data shows that the share of female government recruits has fallen since quotas were cut, shrinking an already limited number of civil service roles held by women.

‘Uncomfortable’

Until 2018, quotas accounted for 56 per cent of Class I posts, the top ranking civil service and public sector jobs.

That included 10pc for women, as well as 30pc for descendants of those who fought for Bangladesh’s independence in 1971.

Another 16pc was reserved for underprivileged regions and people with disabilities.

In 2018, after student protests, the then prime minister Sheikh Hassina scrapped quotas.

In 2024, it was proposed to reinstate quotas, sparking student protests.

That escalated into a mass uprising, and Hasina was overthrown.

Today, 93pc are filled on merit. A 7pc quota is reserved for those related to freedom fighters and other smaller groups, and there is no quota for women.

The Bangladesh Public Service Commission (BPSC), which runs the recruitment examinations, has around 300,000 applicants each year for 2,500-3,000 Class I jobs.

Before the quota was scrapped in 2018, women accounted for up to 35pc of recruits, including both quota and merit-based appointments.

That has dropped to 19pc, according to figures from the last exam round.

A BPSC official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the body “finds the outcome uncomfortable”, but that its “duty is limited to conducting the examination”.

AKM Abdul Awal Majumdar, a former bureaucrat, backs merit-based recruitment but advocates coaching to help women compete.

“My female colleagues were unparallelled,” he said.

The government elected in February also backs merit-based recruitment.

Md Abdul Bari, a public administration minister, described it as a “rational reform” in parliament.

But some officials fear the decline in female recruitment will become increasingly visible.

“At this moment, at least 21 women are leading 21 districts,” said a female bureaucrat with 20 years of experience, speaking on condition of anonymity.

“In 10 years’ time, there won’t be this many women in the service.”

‘Can’t continue’

The impact goes beyond the civil service.

Police data shows that only 267 women out of 2,651 candidates qualified as constables this year.

Only six of the 184 candidates who qualified as police sub-inspectors were women. No women qualified as sergeants, compared with 96 men.

“We can’t continue without them,” a police officer told AFP, noting that every station has dedicated desks for women and children.

Bangladesh previously had 60pc quotas for women in primary teaching positions. That has also ended.

Asif Shahan, a Dhaka University professor of Development Studies, said fewer women in government would impact policymaking.

“Their issues get reflected in policy,” he told AFP.

The debate has split students.

Md Mazharul Islam, a Dhaka University students’ union career advisor, a supporter of the Islamist party Jamaat-e-Islami, backs a merit system.

“Society was much more conservative before, and girls were not allowed to pursue higher education,” he said.

“That has changed.”

Philosophy student Adity Islam said abolishing the women’s quota was wrong.

“We measured women across all walks of life with the yardstick of female students at Dhaka University,” said Islam, who is involved in leftist politics.

“Cutting the quota for women would eventually impact the overall governance system. We have already seen that in some districts. So aspiring candidates in many other places will lose hope.”

Bangladesh Missions abroad go offline due to technical issues with DIP server
item.description:
The government is working to address the technical issues as soon as possible and help the Bangladesh Missions abroad deal with visa processing issues, as the server is currently unavailable.
“Efforts are underway to address the technical issues as soon as possible,” a senior official told UNB on Monday night, noting that due to technical issues with the central system of the Department of Immigration and Passports (DIP), Bangladesh, the MRV (Machine Readable Visa) server is currently unavailable.
He said all the Missions abroad are facing the same problem. A visa applicant who applied from a European country told UNB that he submitted his visa application online but has been unable to proceed with the process due to the technical issue.
“Although the system indicated that I would receive an email within 24 hours of submitting the application, I have not received any email so far, while repeated calls have gone unanswered,” said the applicant.
Due to the technical issues, the processing of NVR (No Visa Required (NVR)) and visa applications and the issuance of visas at the Bangladesh Missions abroad are experiencing a temporary delay.
The Department of Immigration and Passports (DIP), Bangladesh, is working to resolve the technical issues and restore the central system at the earliest possible time.
The government has requested the applicants to allow additional time for the processing of their applications and to refrain from making repeated enquiries regarding the status of their applications during this period.
Meanwhile, the Embassy of Bangladesh, Berlin, in an urgent notice, regretted any inconvenience caused and appreciated the patience, understanding and cooperation of all concerned.
Applicants will be informed via the websites and Facebook pages of the Missions abroad once the central system is restored and normal visa services resume.
Another official said the Department of Immigration and Passports (DIP) conveyed to the Missions abroad the information regarding the technical issues last week, as it is applicable to all.
The Embassy of Bangladesh in Bangkok, in a public message on Tuesday, said it informed all visa service seekers that, due to a temporary technical issue with the visa server, applicants may experience difficulties in submitting visa applications and/or receiving visa-related services.
The embassy said the concerned technical team is working to resolve the issue as soon as possible.
Applicants have been requested to bear with the temporary inconvenience and, where possible, avoid making urgent travel arrangements dependent on immediate visa processing until the system is fully restored.
The embassy regretted the inconvenience caused and appreciated the patience and understanding of all concerned.

item.title: ECNEC approves 13 projects involving Tk 158.24b
item.description:
The Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) today. Tuesday approved 13 development projects involving an estimated cost of Tk 158.24 billion (15,823.57 crore), including a major project to expand the electricity network in the three hill districts.

The approvals was given at the 4th ECNEC meeting of the current fiscal year (FY27), held at the Bangladesh Secretariat with ECNEC Chairman and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman in the chair.

State Minister for Planning Md. Zonayed Abdur Rahim Saki and Planning Division Secretary SM Shakil Akhter briefed reporters after the meeting at the NEC Conference Room in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar.

The electricity network expansion project in the three hill districts will cost Tk 29.10 billion (2,910.22 crore) and will be implemented by the Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) under the Power Division from July 2026 to June 2031.

Of the total project cost, Tk 4.44 billion (444.31 crore) will come from the government's own resources, Tk 20.98 billion (2,098.40 crore) from project loans and Tk 3.68 billion (367.52 crore) from the implementing organisation's own funds.

The project is aimed at expanding electricity distribution infrastructure in the three hill districts, improving access to electricity and strengthening the power network in the remote and hilly areas.

The ECNEC also approved a Tk 211-million (21.14 crore) project for acquiring land for construction of a solar power plant at Sonagazi in Feni district. The project will be implemented by the Electricity Generation Company of Bangladesh (EGCB) Ltd from July 2026 to June 2028.

Among the other approved projects, the largest allocation went to widening and strengthening important upazila and union roads in Rangpur Division, involving Tk 49.50 billion (4,949.76 crore).

The project will be implemented by the Local Government Engineering Department (LGED) from July 2026 to June 2030 with government funding.

The ECNEC also approved the Tk 40.39-billion (4,039.06 crore) Integrated Health System Response to Fight TB, HIV/AIDS and Malaria in Bangladesh project.

Of the amount, Tk 31.69 billion (3,168.89 crore) will come from government resources and Tk 8.70 billio (870.18 crore) from project grant/loan. The project will run from July 2026 to June 2029.

Another major project approved today is the Tk 12.76-billion (1,276.30 crore) Financial Sector Support Project-II (FSSP-II), to be implemented by Bangladesh Bank from July 2026 to June 2031. The project will receive Tk 12.62 billion (1,261.54 crore) as project loan and Tk 147.6 million (14.76 crore) from Bangladesh Bank's own funds.

The ECNEC approved the 3rd revised Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport Expansion Project (Phase 1), raising its total revised cost to Tk 222.13 billion (22,213.09 crore), an increase of Tk 8.48 billion (847.57 crore). The project is scheduled for completion by June 2027.

Two water-resource projects were also approved. One involves Tk 7.52 billion (751.77 crore) for integrated flood and river management and drainage improvement in the Small Feni and Bamni river basin, including construction of the Musapur Regulator (Part-1).

The other, involving Tk 6.05 billion (605.24 crore), aims to protect Shibpur, Dhaniya and Medua areas under Bhola Sadar and Daulatkhan upazilas from erosion of the Meghna River.

The ECNEC also approved Tk 3.08 billion (308.30 crore) for expanding existing physical disability training centres in Chattogram, Khulna and Rajshahi divisions and enhancing the capacity of the Neuro-Developmental Disabled (NDD) Children's Institute at Rofabad in Chattogram, including construction of a hostel building.

A Tk 5.05-billion (505.32 crore) revised project for conducting land surveys in three city corporations, one pourashava and 2 rural upazilas through digital methods was also approved.

Besides, the ECNEC approved the revised project for strengthening the technical and technological capacity of the Special Response Battalion (SRB), with the total revised cost reduced by Tk 89.9 million (8.99 crore) to Tk 3.43 billion (343.24 crore).

The ECNEC also approved the 3rd revised Rural Infrastructure Development Project in Madaripur, Shariatpur and Rajbari districts, raising its total cost to Tk 25.15 billion (2,515.27 crore).

The establishment of Patuakhali Medical College and Hospital was also given an extension of implementation period, with its revised cost standing at Tk 6.51 billion (651.01 crore).

Of the 13 approved projects, eight are new projects, three are revised schemes and two are proposals for extension of implementation periods without cost revisions.

The ECNEC was also informed about 15 development projects, each costing below Tk 500 million (50 crore), that had earlier been approved by the Planning Minister.

The 15 projects include vertical expansion of Bangladesh International School and College, Nirjhor; improvement of education quality and teaching capacity at BAF Shaheen College, Kurmitola; infrastructure development at Alikadam Cantonment Public School and College; establishment and infrastructure development of government primary schools in Dhaka City and Purbachal; establishment of BSTI regional offices in 10 districts; the Rupsha 800 MW Combined Cycle Power Plant; establishment of the Mirpur UCEP-Labor and Employment Institute and human resource development;

The Climate-Smart Agriculture and Water Management project; flood control and left- and right-bank protection of the Dharla River in Kurigram; protection of both banks of the Kushiyara River in front of the Bibiyana power plants in Habiganj; improvement of civic services, roads and drainage in Mymensingh City Corporation;

Safe water supply across the country; water supply and sanitation in 23 unicipalities; upgrading of the Bhuapur-Tarakandi district highway (Z-4801); and surface water treatment, piped water supply and safe sanitation in Chapainawabganj Municipality.

item.title: Govt holiday extended by a day, giving 5-day break, PM also increases grants
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has increased grants for the Hindu community’s Sharadiya Durga Puja and the Buddhist community’s religious festival.

The Hindu Religious Welfare Trust had sought Tk 40 million for Durga Puja, but Tk 50 million was allocated at the prime minister’s special consideration.

Similarly, the Buddhist Religious Welfare Trust had sought Tk 20 million for the Kathin Chibar Dan ceremony, but Tk 30 million was allocated at the prime minister’s special consideration.

Every year, the Hindu Religious Welfare Trust receives an allocation from state funds for the Sharadiya Durga Puja. This year, the prime minister has increased that allocation by Tk 10 million.

25 September was the second-largest religious festival of the Buddhist community, Probarana Purnima. On this occasion, Tk 10 million more than the amount requested was also allocated for the Kathin Chibar Dan ceremony.

This year, the holiday for Sharadiya Durga Puja is also being extended.

According to the government’s holiday calendar, Tuesday, 20 October, will be a holiday by executive order on the occasion of Navami. Wednesday, 21 October, will be a general holiday for Bijoya Dashami.

Government offices and courts were scheduled to reopen on Thursday, 22 October.

However, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman announced today that 22 October would also be a holiday. 23 and 24 October are Friday and Saturday, the weekly holidays. As a result, government employees will enjoy five consecutive days off from 20 to 24 October.


Banks and financial institutions are also generally closed on government holidays. However, specific branches or special services may remain open in accordance with Bangladesh Bank directives. Digital services such as ATMs, cards and online banking generally remain operational.

Employees engaged in essential services such as hospitals, police, fire service, electricity, gas and water supply, however, will have to remain on duty during the holidays. Employees at some necessary institutions, including media organisations, may also be required to work.

The five-day holiday around Durga Puja will give members of the Hindu community more opportunity to celebrate the festival. The government has also allocated more than the requested amounts in grants. Bijon Kanti Sarkar, special assistant to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Hindu, Buddhist, Christian and ethnic minority affairs, described the prime minister’s initiative as a different example of sincerity.

Speaking to Prothom Alo, he said, “The prime minister has added one day to the holiday, but we are getting five days off in total. This will make the festival more complete and comfortable. And by providing grants beyond what was requested, the prime minister’s favourable attitude towards Hindus, Buddhists, Christians and all communities has been demonstrated. This is very positive."

item.title: Officials: Maitree Express journey time may fall to 6 hours via Padma Bridge
item.description:
The journey time of Maitree Express between Dhaka and Kolkata could be reduced by around three to six hours if the cross-border passenger train is operated through the Padma Bridge-Benapole route instead of the existing Jamuna Bridge-Darsana route, officials said.
The proposed route could also reduce the passenger fare by around Tk1,000, making the train a more convenient alternative to air travel between the two cities, according to sources familiar with the matter.
The Maitree Express, which connects Bangladesh and India, was suspended on July 19, 2024, amid security concerns.
Despite recent political tensions between the two neighbouring countries, the number of Bangladeshi tourists entering India jumped by nearly 80% compared with the corresponding period of the previous year.
According to preliminary data by the Ministry of Tourism, India, over 74,000 people from Bangladesh travelled to India in August.
On September 9, Railways Minister Shaikh Rabiul Alam informed Parliament that freight train services are currently operating between Bangladesh and India, while initiatives are being taken to resume passenger train services with the neighbouring country.
Railway Ministry Additional Secretary Ziaul Haque, after the three-day recent inter-governmental railway meeting, told the reporters that no decision has been taken yet on resuming the suspended cross-border train services between Bangladesh and India.
Officials said the two sides are reviewing the possibility of restarting the train services.
The train - Maitree Express - was introduced jointly by Bangladesh and India in April 2008, on the occasion of the Bengali New Year, with the aim of restoring passenger rail connectivity between the two countries that had been disrupted in 1965.
The cross-border service has since served as an important mode of transport for passengers travelling between Bangladesh and India, particularly those travelling for tourism, trade, commerce and medical treatment.
According to Bangladesh Railway sources, a total of 288,360 passengers travelled on Maitree Express from 2022-23 until July 19, 2024. Available records show that around 95% of the passengers were from Bangladesh.
The train maintained an average occupancy rate of 80 to 85%, while the occupancy exceeded 95% during major holidays such as Eid and Durga Puja, reflecting strong demand for the service among Bangladeshi passengers.
Under the existing arrangement for cross-border passenger train operations, Bangladesh Railway receives 75% of the apportioned earnings from passenger bookings on Maitree Express, while the remaining 25% goes to Indian Railways.
Before its suspension, Maitree Express operated through the Tangail-Jamuna Bridge-Ishwardi-Darsana route, covering around 392 kilometres between Dhaka and Kolkata.
According to the approved timetable, the train departed Dhaka Station at 8:15am and was scheduled to reach Kolkata at 4pm, taking seven hours and 45 minutes. On the return journey, it departed Kolkata's Chitpur Terminal Station at 7:10am and was scheduled to arrive in Dhaka at 3:35pm, taking eight hours and 25 minutes.
In practice, however, the journey could take more than nine to 10 hours due to congestion on the railway network, particularly along the Dhaka-Ishwardi-Darsana section.
The opening of the Padma Bridge railway route in December 2024 has created an alternative corridor for trains travelling towards the country's southwestern region and the Benapole border.
The distance and travel time between Kamlapur and Benapole have been significantly reduced through the new route.
While trains previously required more than eight hours for the journey, Ruposhi Bangla Express now covers the route in around three hours and four minutes, according to railway sources.
Railway officials believe Maitree Express could similarly benefit if it is rerouted through Padma Bridge and Benapole instead of the Jamuna Bridge-Darsana corridor.

item.description: Over the last half millennium, societies around the globe competed to divide up the world’s land. Nearly every square inch of soil outside Antarctica is now owned and tucked within national borders. But the oceans have largely been spared that fate. There were times throughout history when countries tried to gate and regulate the seas, but they were too vast to be controlled for long periods. During the Cold War, as technology made it far easier to imagine partitioning the world’s waterways and seabeds, great powers avoided an unrestrained race to grab the oceans. Most governments agreed to deal with them through a patchwork of treaties and multilateral bodies that sought to guarantee freedom of navigation in international waters and assign coastal seabeds to adjacent littoral states.

item.title: From Taiwan to Takaichi, the geopolitical fallout from Xi-Trump summit
The Houthis Took the Red Sea Coast. How Did Washington Miss It?
item.description:
The recent military moves taken by Yemens Houthis resulted in stunning victories and significant strategic gains, virtually unopposed. By taking the Red Sea port of Mocha (Al-Makha), occupying Perim Island in the middle of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, and seizing portions of the Red Sea coast, the Iranian proxy group now threatens a key commercial waterway. Reports indicate that, unsurprisingly – or at least it should not be a surprise – Iranian Revolutionary Guard advisors were present, guiding the tactics of Houthi forces. We missed all of this.

For decades, the United States has had an active, robust CIA, diplomatic, and military presence in the Persian Gulf. Understanding, managing, and balancing the nuanced and sometimes fractious relationships among our Gulf allies has always been a complicated task, but one critical to the national security of both the United States and our Gulf allies. We have all made it work, together.

Until now. Something has gone terribly wrong.

As a former CIA operations officer and Chief of Station in the Gulf, I know that failing to anticipate an Iranian-Houthi move of this magnitude is not a tactical error or simply failing to “connect the dots.” Regional actors have their own specific interests and goals in Yemen. Each has taken its turn in the barrel militarily, seemingly largely uncoordinated and sometimes at odds with one another, to discourage or defeat the Houthis. None has succeeded.

What is lacking is leadership, coordination, and overall command and control among the key players: Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and the United States. And in the latter’s case, lack of focus.

The current regional conflict seems to have opened rifts in the alliances all of us who served in the Gulf and greater Middle East strove so painstakingly to build and nurture. This is not necessarily through a simple lack of presence or communication; the Commander of CENTCOM was just recently there for consultations, and I have no doubt U.S. military personnel on the ground are in constant and very close contact with their Gulf counterparts. And from my own time there, I am certain U.S. diplomatic and intelligence personnel are equally engaged. This is what we do, and we all do it well.

So how did we miss the Houthi move?

Let’s be clear. This stuff is hard. Anticipating the plans and intentions of an adversary is one of the most important things the intelligence community, and specifically the CIA, does. And the U.S. military has no peer in its planning, logistics, or execution capabilities.

But it is really difficult to anticipate and address the actions of an adversary that relies heavily on asymmetrical warfare.

Particularly when you are dealing with not one but two denied area foes–the U.S. does not have an operational Embassy in either Iran or Yemen. But it can be done; I’ve done it. It just takes focus and, yes, imagination.

But it is important to remember that the intelligence, military, and Diplomatic communities do not operate in a vacuum. Each reports to and receives direction from the White House and DoD. Based on my understanding of how these operate and interact, I can only surmise that the confusion we have seen is emanating from the very top.

Or perhaps an inability, or unwillingness, to manage yet another military crisis.

The U.S.’s lurch into war alongside Israel, one with no apparent end-game, seemingly caught the Gulf Monarchies by surprise. They have suffered the consequences, both militarily and economically. Perhaps ‘Operation Economic Outcast’ - the U.S.’s current intense financial offensive against Iran - will finally bring the Iranian regime to the table to negotiate in good faith. But that remains to be seen. And the Iranians continue to surprise us.

I’ll leave it to others more intimately versed in things Yemeni to analyze the Houthi tactics and strategic goals.

But it should be no surprise that Iran called on the Houthis to make a move at this time. Both the Iranians, and now the Houthis, have proven themselves to be master opportunists. One succeeded in opening a second front in an attempt to lessen the pressure of the U.S. naval blockade and increased sanctions, and the other saw an opportunity to expand their reach. A distracted Washington gave them the opening.

The takeaway: Overconfidence in the ultimate efficacy of Operation Economic Outcast may turn out to be misplaced. If the success of the Houthi advance does not turn out to be an isolated incident, it risks exposing a critical vulnerability in the United States’ strategy. Washington needs to keep its eye on the ball.
